edbDesc: The tendency for the peak luminance sensitivity of the human eye to shift toward the blue end of the color spectrum at low illumination levels.This effect introduces a difference in color contrast under different levels of illumination.
title: Purkinje effect
description: As light fades at dusk, reds look darker and blues and greens look brighter, because the eye switches from colour-sensing cones to rods, which see blue-green best and red hardly at all. Jan Purkyně noticed it in 1819 when red flowers in his garden turned dark at dawn while the leaves stayed bright. It is why red lamps protect night vision in submarines, ship bridges and observatories, and why bluish-white street lights look brighter at night.
effect: in dim light the eye becomes more sensitive to blue-green and nearly blind to red
usedIn: Red night lighting in submarines, ship bridges and observatories
Street-lighting standards that rate lamps for night-time (mesopic) vision
strength: In near-darkness the eye's peak sensitivity shifts from yellow-green (555 nm) to blue-green (507 nm), so deep red becomes nearly invisible to the rods.
pickWhy: Borderline: Judgment call: a quirk of human vision rather than a physical effect a device exploits; picked keep because it guides real lighting design, but drop is defensible.
